labs.title: IDOR — read another customer's account
labs.exploit: Log in as alice, then change the id in the request path to bob's account. The response body is bob's account — balances, owner, everything.
labs.hint: The service fetches the account by id and returns it without ever asking whether the caller owns it. Compare the account's owner id against the authenticated principal.

labs.title: Privilege escalation — customer reaches the admin API
labs.exploit: Log in as alice and call the admin endpoint with her token. It answers 200 and lists every user, password hashes included — because the matcher only requires an authenticated caller.
labs.hint: The matcher for /api/admin/** says .authenticated(). It needs a role requirement.

labs.title: SSRF — make the server fetch an internal URL
labs.exploit: Ask for a statement to be emailed to a URL you control, and point that URL at an internal address. The server fetches it on your behalf and the response tells you what came back.
labs.hint: The callback URL goes straight into an HTTP client with no allowlist and no check on the resolved address.

labs.title: Debug mode — the stack trace exposes the JWT secret and DB credentials
labs.exploit: Call the debug endpoint. The exception message and the stack trace carry the signing secret and the JDBC connection string.
labs.hint: Two halves: the exception message embeds the secrets, and server.error.include-* is set to always so the trace is rendered.

labs.title: Default admin credentials — admin/admin opens the operations console
labs.exploit: Log in to the operations console with admin / admin. Those are the credentials the code compares against, and they are also what the seed data sets.
labs.hint: The controller compares the submitted password against a literal. Compare against the stored hash instead, and rotate the seeded password.

labs.title: Sensitive file exposure — .env, .git/config and backup.zip on the web root
labs.exploit: Fetch the files directly. They are sitting in the static resource root, which Spring serves to anyone.
labs.hint: These files are in the served static root. Move them outside it — the fix is to take them off the web root entirely.

labs.title: Unsalted MD5 password hashes — crack them offline in seconds
labs.exploit: Pull the stored hashes and run them through a rainbow table. MD5 is unsalted, so identical passwords collide and the whole table falls at once.
labs.hint: Swap the hasher for bcrypt or Argon2, and re-seed with salted hashes. The salt must be per-user and stored alongside the hash.

labs.title: Hardcoded JWT secret — forge an admin token
labs.exploit: Read the secret out of the source (or out of the Lab 4 stack trace), sign your own token with role=admin, and send it. The server trusts the signature.
labs.hint: The secret is a string literal in the source tree, and it is logged at startup. It needs to come from configuration or the environment, with real entropy.

labs.title: PII in cleartext — the profile endpoint returns unmasked customer data
labs.exploit: Call the endpoint and read the response. Full names, dates of birth, national IDs — unmasked, and the same data is written to the log.
labs.hint: Mask the sensitive fields before they leave the process, and keep them out of the log line.

labs.title: SQL injection — bypass the login and dump the users table
labs.exploit: Log in with the username admin' -- and any password. The quote closes the string and the comment removes the rest of the WHERE clause, so the admin row comes back with no password check at all.
labs.hint: The username is pasted into the SQL string. Use a parameterized query and let the driver handle the quoting.

labs.title: SpEL injection — the remark is evaluated as an expression
labs.exploit: Set the remark to 7*7 and it comes back as 49 — your input was evaluated. (Note: #{7*7} does NOT work — #{...} is template syntax, and parseExpression() takes a bare expression.) Push it further with T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec(...) and you have code execution.
labs.hint: The fix is the standard idiom: the template is a constant and the user input arrives as a variable.

labs.title: SSTI + OS command injection — read internal config and run commands
labs.exploit: Two bugs in two methods. The report template is evaluated as an expression, and the date filter is concatenated into a shell command, so a quote lets you run whatever you like.
labs.hint: Two separate methods, two separate fixes. For the shell: pass arguments as a list, never as one string to sh -c.

labs.title: Stored XSS — a transaction note is rendered as raw HTML
labs.exploit: Send a transfer whose note is . It is stored and later injected into the DOM with dangerouslySetInnerHTML, so it executes in every browser that views the transaction.
labs.hint: Escape the value in the renderer before it becomes markup. Note that the React app injects the raw note with dangerouslySetInnerHTML, so fix TransfersPage.tsx too — the server-side fix alone will not protect the browser.

labs.title: Negative transfer — the amount is applied without validation
labs.exploit: Send a negative amount. The same amount is added to both accounts, so both lose the money and the total in the system changes — which is the invariant that must never break.
labs.hint: Validate the amount before the arithmetic: it must be positive, and it must not exceed the balance.

labs.title: Mass assignment — promote yourself to admin via the profile endpoint
labs.exploit: Send {"role":"admin"} in the profile update body. The request is bound straight onto the entity, so your own account is rewritten.
labs.hint: Bind to a dedicated update DTO that has only the fields a client is allowed to change.

labs.title: Account enumeration — the login error tells you if a user exists
labs.exploit: Compare the error messages. "User not found" and "Incorrect password" are different strings, so you can tell valid usernames from invalid ones without any credentials.
labs.hint: Return one indistinguishable message for both cases, and make the two paths take the same time.

labs.title: Brute force — the login endpoint never locks the account out
labs.exploit: Try weak passwords against one account in a loop. Nothing counts the failures and nothing refuses the request, so the sweep runs to the end.
labs.hint: Three edits: the service must refuse once the budget is gone, a failed login must count, and a successful login must clear the counter.

labs.title: Session fixation — the session id survives login unchanged
labs.exploit: Get a session id before logging in, log in as the victim with that id in the cookie, and the id stays valid afterwards. The attacker already holds it.
labs.hint: Rotate the session id on login. Spring Security does this by default — the lab disables it with sessionFixation(none()).

labs.title: Predictable reset token — compute it offline from the username
labs.exploit: The reset token is md5(username + unixTimestamp). You know the username, and the timestamp is the second the request was made, so you can compute the token yourself.
labs.hint: Use a cryptographically random token, store it with an expiry, and invalidate it after use.

labs.title: Unsafe deserialization — an upload becomes remote code execution
labs.exploit: Upload a serialized Java object whose readObject runs a command. The server deserializes it and your command executes on the host.
labs.hint: Do not deserialize untrusted bytes. If you must, use a filter that allowlists classes — or accept JSON.

labs.title: JWT alg:none — forge an admin token with no key at all
labs.exploit: Set the header's alg to none, leave the signature empty, and claim role=admin. The parser never looks at alg and never checks the signature.
labs.hint: Use a library parser that pins the algorithm and verifies the signature. jjwt's parseSignedClaims rejects alg:none outright.

labs.title: Unrestricted file upload — your file, your name, served as HTML
labs.exploit: Upload an .html file. It keeps your filename, lands in the served uploads directory, and is handed back with a text/html content type — so it runs in the bank's origin.
labs.hint: Generate the stored name yourself, drop the original extension, and serve uploads as application/octet-stream from outside the web root.

labs.title: Verbose error — the stack trace tells the attacker how the app works
labs.exploit: Send a non-numeric id. The response carries the exception class, the package layout, and every frame of the call stack.
labs.hint: Catch the parse failure and return a clean 400. Turn off the global stack-trace inclusion too.

labs.title: Type coercion — the error message names your classes and fields
labs.exploit: Send amount as a string. The binding error comes back verbatim and tells the attacker the DTO's package, class name, and field list.
labs.hint: Handle HttpMessageNotReadableException yourself and return a generic message. This one has its own handler, so it is independent of Lab 23.

labs.title: Fail-open authentication — a token that names nobody becomes the admin
labs.exploit: Get a service token from the app. It is valid and correctly signed — it just does not say who the bearer is. The filter cannot establish an identity, so it falls through to the default, and user_id 1 is the admin.
labs.hint: The filter must fail closed: a token that names no identity is a 401, not a default principal.
